## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

```{r install-tinytex, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("tinytex")
```

```{r example1}
# Example 1: create numeric vectors and summarise them
# Create x with two numbers
x <- c(0.5, 0.6)
# Create age with four ages
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)
# Show min, max, mean, median and quartiles of age
summary(age)
```

```{r example2}
# Example 2: calculate the mean of a numeric vector
age<-c(35,24,18,24)
mean(age)
```

```{r logical}
# Logical vectors: values are TRUE / FALSE (or T / F)
x <- c(TRUE,FALSE)
x <- c(T, F)
```

```{r character}
# Character vectors: text values written in quotes
x <- c("a", "b", "c" )
class<-c("M","F","F","M")
```

```{r integer}
# Integer vectors: whole numbers made with the : operator
x <- 9:29
```

```{r complex}
# Complex vectors: numbers with a real and an imaginary part
x <- c(1+0i, 2+4i)
```

```{r matrix}
# Matrices: create two matrices and multiply them with %*%
(x<- matrix(1:6,nrow = 2,ncol = 3))
(y<-matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2))
x%*%y
```

```{r list}
# List: one object that can hold values of different types
(x <- list(1, "a", TRUE, 1 + 4i))
x
```

```{r factor-missing}
# 1. Factors (categories) and missing values (NA)
# Create a factor (categories: yes / no)
x <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"))

# Create a vector with a missing value (NA)
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)

# Check which values are NA
is.na(x)

# "NA" in quotes is text, not a missing value
x <- c(1, 2, 4, "NA", 5)
bad <- is.na(x)
print(bad)

# Keep only values that are not NA
x[!bad]

# Keep rows with no missing values in x and y
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, 5)
y <- c("a", "b", NA, "d", NA, "f")
good <- complete.cases(x, y)
good
```

```{r coercion}
# 2. Coercion: R converts TRUE/FALSE to 1/0 when doing maths
# TRUE = 1 and FALSE = 0, so the sum counts the TRUE values
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))
```

```{r data-frame}
# 3. Create a data frame (table) from vectors
# Create the columns
studentID <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
math_score <- c(12, 17, 10, 9, NA)
gender <- c("M", "F", "M", "M", "F")
it_score <- c(13, 18, 11, 10, 19)

# Join the columns into one table
scoredata <- data.frame(studentID, gender, math_score, it_score)
scoredata

# Open the table in a viewer window
View(scoredata)
```

```{r summary-stats}
# 8. Summary statistics: mean and standard deviation
# Mean of each row (1 = rows)
apply(data_class, 1, mean)

# Standard deviation of each column (2 = columns)
apply(data_class, 2, sd)

# Mean and SD of HEIGHT
c(mean(data_class$HEIGHT), sd(data_class$HEIGHT))

# Mean and SD of WEIGHT
c(mean(data_class$WEIGHT), sd(data_class$WEIGHT))

# Same, but with labels
c(Mean = mean(data_class$HEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
c(Mean = mean(data_class$WEIGHT), SD = sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
```

```{r iris}
# 9. Compare a number across categories (iris data)
# Load and look at the iris data
data("iris")
head(iris)

# Mean petal length for all flowers
mean(iris$Petal.Length)

# Mean petal length for each species
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "virginica"])

# Shortcut: mean, SD and summary by species
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)

# Boxplot: compare sepal length by species
boxplot(iris$Sepal.Length ~ iris$Species, data = iris,
        main = "Comparison of categorical vs quantitative")
```

```{r ucb-admissions}
# 10. Compare two categories with a cross table (UCB admissions)
# Turn the admissions data into a table
ucba <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucba)

# Count admitted and rejected by gender
cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba)
(cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba))

# Show percentages by gender (each row adds to 1)
prop.table(cross, 1)
```

```{r simpson}
# 11. Simpson's paradox: the result changes inside one department
# Same table, but only for department F
cross2 <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba[ucba$Dept == "F", ])
prop.table(cross2, 1)
```

```{r scatter-plots}
# 13. Scatter plots and correlation
# Three ways to plot weight vs height
#plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
#plot(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
# plot(data_class[, 1], data_class[, 2], main = "Graph")
# Way 1: formula style (y ~ x)
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)

# Way 2: use column names with $
plot(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)

# Way 3: use column numbers (1st column = x, 2nd column = y) and add a title
plot(data_class[, 1], data_class[, 2], main = "Graph")

# Correlation between height and weight
cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
```

```{r linear-model}
# 14. Linear model: fit a straight line and check it
# Scatter plot with a straight line
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)$coefficient)

# Model: predict height from weight
data_lm <- lm(HEIGHT ~ WEIGHT, data = data_class)
summary(data_lm)

# Check the model with diagnostic plots (press Enter in Console for next plot)
plot(data_lm)

# Histograms
hist(data_class$HEIGHT)
hist(data_class$WEIGHT, col = "blue")
```

```{r straight-curved-line}
# 15. Add a straight line and a smooth curved line to a plot
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)$coefficient)

# Add a smooth curved line in blue
lines(lowess(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT), col = "blue")

cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)

# Show the model coefficients
lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
```

```{r bmi}
# 16. Create a new variable (BMI) and add it to the table
# Use column names directly (no need for data_class$)
attach(data_class)

# Calculate BMI
(BMI <- WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2)

# BMI rounded to 2 decimals
(BMI <- round(WEIGHT / (HEIGHT / 100)^2, digit = 2))

# Add BMI as a new column and show first 5 rows
head(cbind(data_class, BMI), n = 5)

# Save the new table
new_data_class <- cbind(data_class, BMI)

# Show last 10 rows
tail(cbind(data_class, BMI), n = 10)
```

```{r bmi-summary}
# 17. Summary of BMI and a stem-and-leaf plot
summary(BMI)

# Stem-and-leaf plot
stem(BMI, scale = 2)
```

```{r dates}
# 18. Working with dates
# Today's date
today <- Sys.Date()

# Show date as "Month day year"
format(today, format = "%B %d %Y")

# Show the day name
format(today, format = "%A")

# Number of days since a birth date
today <- Sys.Date()
dob <- as.Date("1982-02-10")
difftime(today, dob, units = "days")

# Days between two dates
startdate <- as.Date("2004-02-13")
enddate <- as.Date("2011-01-22")
days <- enddate - startdate
days
```

```{r leadership}
# 19. Create the leadership data frame
# Create the columns
manager <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
country <- c("US", "US", "UK", "UK", "UK")
gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F")
age <- c(32, 45, 25, 39, 99)
q1 <- c(5, 3, 3, 3, 2)
q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2)
q3 <- c(5, 2, 5, 4, 1)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 5, NA, 2)
q5 <- c(5, 5, 2, NA, 1)

# Join into a table (text as factors)
leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age, q1, q2, q3, q4, q5,
                         stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

# Join into a table (text stays as text)
leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age, q1, q2, q3, q4, q5)

str(leadership)
names(leadership)
```

```{r missing-age-groups}
# 20. Recode missing values and create age groups
# Age 99 means missing, so change it to NA
leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA
View(leadership)

# Create age groups
leadership$agecat[leadership$age > 75] <- "Elder"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75] <- "Middle Aged"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age < 35] <- "Young"

# Check missing values in q1 to q5
is.na(leadership[, 5:9])

# Remove rows with any missing value
newdata <- na.omit(leadership)
newdata
```

```{r sorting}
# 21. Sort rows of a data frame
# Order of rows from youngest to oldest
order(leadership$age)

# Sort the table by age
newdata2 <- leadership[order(leadership$age), ]
```

```{r select-columns-rows}
# 22. Select and remove columns and rows
# Keep columns 5 to 9
newdata3 <- leadership[, c(5:9)]

# Keep columns by name
myvars <- c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")
(newdata3 <- leadership[myvars])

# Remove columns 1 and 2
newdata4 <- leadership[, c(-1, -2)]

# Remove columns 1 to 5
(newdata4 <- leadership[, -(1:5)])

# Remove columns 1 and 7
newdata5 <- leadership[, c(-1, -7)]

# Two ways to get the age column
leadership[[4]]
leadership$age

# Remove rows 1 and 3
newdata6 <- leadership[c(-1, -3), ]

# Keep rows 2, 4 and 5
newdata6 <- leadership[c(2, 4, 5), ]

# Keep q1-q5 for people aged 35+ or under 24
newdata7 <- subset(leadership, age >= 35 | age < 24,
                   select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5))

# Use column names directly
attach(leadership)

# Keep men older than 30
(newdata7 <- leadership[gender == "M" & age > 30, ])

# Stop using column names directly
detach(leadership)
```
